First, $R_m$ is orthogonal, so RoPE preserves $\|q\|$ exactly — it cannot inflate or damp logits, which is why it composes safely with the normalization schemes of Chapter 12. Second, the logit is a sum of $d_h/2$ sinusoids in the relative distance, with frequencies spanning $\theta_0 = 1$ down to $\theta_{63} = 10^{-3.94}$ for $d_h=128$, $b=10^4$ — not quite four orders of magnitude, or wavelengths from $6.28$ to $5.44\times10^4$ tokens; the low-frequency pairs carry coarse long-range position and the high-frequency pairs carry fine local order.

Why this family and not some other? Because it is the only one.

Theorem 19.2 (Uniqueness of the rotary form)

Suppose position acts linearly, $q_m \mapsto A_m q$, $k_n \mapsto A_n k$, with $A_0 = I$, $m \mapsto A_m$ continuous, and suppose $\langle A_m q, A_n k\rangle$ depends on $(m,n)$ only through $n-m$ for all $q,k$. Then in some orthonormal basis $A_m$ is block-diagonal with $2\times2$ rotation blocks (plus possible fixed coordinates), i.e. exactly Definition 19.1 up to a change of basis and a choice of the $\theta_i$.

Proof sketch. The hypothesis forces $A_m^\top A_n = A_0^\top A_{n-m} = A_{n-m}$ as bilinear forms, hence as matrices. Setting $n=m$ gives $A_m^\top A_m = A_0 = I$, so every $A_m$ is orthogonal. Substituting back, $A_n = A_m A_{n-m}$, i.e. $A_{s+t} = A_s A_t$: the family is a continuous one-parameter subgroup of $O(d_h)$, so $A_m = \exp(mS)$ with $S$ real skew-symmetric. Every real skew-symmetric matrix is orthogonally similar to a block-diagonal form with blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0 & -\theta_i\\ \theta_i & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and zeros, and exponentiating those blocks gives planar rotations by $m\theta_i$. $\blacksquare$

This is the honest answer to "why did rotary win." Any norm-preserving linear encoding of position that makes the dot product translation-invariant is a set of planar rotations. The design space is not "which encoding," it is only "which frequencies $\theta_i$" — and that is precisely the knob every method in Section 19.5 turns.

Common Pitfall

Build the $\cos/\sin$ cache in low precision and long context breaks silently. The angle $m\theta_i$ is formed before the trigonometric call, so at $m \approx 10^6$ a float32 position has $\approx 10^{-1}$ absolute resolution in the phase of the fastest pair. In the artifact, evaluating $\langle R_m q, R_n k\rangle$ at fixed $m-n=1000$ for $m \in \{0, 4096, 131072, 2^{20}\}$ gives a spread of $1.4\times10^{-10}$ in float64 and $7.4\times10^{-2}$ in float32 — the relative-position property, the entire reason for using RoPE, is destroyed at the scale of a real logit. Compute the inverse-frequency vector and the angle table in float64 (or at minimum float32 from an int64 position index) and cast to bfloat16 only after the $\cos$ and $\sin$. Mainstream implementations now force this region out of autocast for exactly this reason. Verify A second, quieter version: the RoFormer paper pairs coordinate $2i$ with $2i+1$, while GPT-NeoX, Llama and most deployed kernels pair $j$ with $j + d_h/2$. The two are the same operator conjugated by a fixed permutation (the artifact confirms agreement to $4.4\times10^{-16}$), so attention scores are unaffected if the same convention is used for $q$ and $k$ — but converting a checkpoint between conventions requires permuting $W_Q$ and $W_K$ rows, and skipping that produces a model that trains and does not obviously crash.

19.5 Context Extension: PI, NTK-aware, YaRN

A model trained at $T_{\text{train}}$ has seen pair $i$ rotate through angles in $[0, T_{\text{train}}\theta_i)$. If $\lambda_i > T_{\text{train}}$ that interval is less than a full turn, and evaluating at $m > T_{\text{train}}$ pushes the pair into angles it has never seen. If $\lambda_i \ll T_{\text{train}}$ the pair has already wrapped hundreds of times and every angle is familiar. This single observation organises the whole field.

Definition 19.2 (Rotation count)

For scale factor $s = T_{\text{target}}/T_{\text{train}}$, the rotation count of pair $i$ is $r_i = T_{\text{train}}/\lambda_i = T_{\text{train}}\theta_i/(2\pi)$: the number of full turns pair $i$ completes inside the trained context.

Position interpolation (PI) rescales positions, $m \mapsto m/s$, equivalently $\theta_i \mapsto \theta_i/s$ for every $i$. Positions in $[0, T_{\text{target}})$ now map into the trained angular range for all pairs, and a short fine-tune (on the order of $10^3$ steps) recovers quality. The cost is indiscriminate: the high-frequency pairs, which encode adjacency, are compressed by $s$ as well, so tokens one apart now differ by the angle that tokens $1/s$ apart used to. Local discrimination degrades, and that is what PI's fine-tuning has to repair.

NTK-aware scaling refuses to touch the fastest pair and applies the full $1/s$ only to the slowest, by raising the base: $b' = b\, s^{d_h/(d_h-2)}$. Check the endpoints: $\theta'_i/\theta_i = (b'/b)^{-2i/d_h} = s^{-\frac{d_h}{d_h-2}\cdot\frac{2i}{d_h}}$, which is $1$ at $i=0$ and exactly $s^{-1}$ at $i = d_h/2-1$. The artifact asserts both endpoints to $10^{-12}$. The interpolation is a smooth geometric sweep in between — principled at the ends, arbitrary in the middle, and it does not know where $T_{\text{train}}$ is.

YaRN makes the middle a function of $r_i$. Define the ramp $\gamma(r) = \mathrm{clip}\!\left(\frac{r-\alpha}{\beta-\alpha}, 0, 1\right)$ and set

$$\theta'_i = \big(1-\gamma(r_i)\big)\frac{\theta_i}{s} + \gamma(r_i)\,\theta_i .$$

Pairs with $r_i < \alpha$ — those that never complete one turn in training — are fully interpolated; pairs with $r_i > \beta$ — already wrapped $\beta$ times — are left exactly alone; the band between ramps linearly. For the Llama family $\alpha = 1$, $\beta = 32$. YaRN additionally scales attention logits by $\sqrt{1/t} = 0.1\ln s + 1$, which counteracts the entropy increase from attending over more tokens; at $s=8$ that factor is $1.2079$. Verify

Example 19.1 (Which pairs get interpolated, by hand)

Take $d_h=128$, $b=10^4$, $T_{\text{train}}=4096$, $s=8$. Pair $i=45$: $\theta_{45} = 10000^{-90/128} = 10^{-2.8125} = 1.5399\times10^{-3}$, so $\lambda_{45} = 2\pi/\theta_{45} = 4080.2$ tokens and $r_{45} = 4096/4080.2 = 1.0039$. That is a hair above $\alpha=1$, so $\gamma = 0.0039/31 = 1.25\times10^{-4}$, giving $\theta'_{45}/\theta_{45} = 0.125 + 0.875\gamma = 0.12511$ — pair 45 is interpolated to within $0.09\%$ of the full $1/s = 0.125$. Pair $i=20$: $\lambda_{20} = 2\pi\cdot 10000^{40/128} = 111.7$ tokens, $r_{20} = 36.66 > 32$, so $\gamma=1$ and YaRN leaves it untouched. The artifact's table reproduces exactly these numbers and reports the partition: 21 pairs untouched, 25 ramped, 18 fully interpolated. PI interpolates all 64 — including the 21 that had no problem.

19.6 Base-Frequency Changes in Practice

The cheapest intervention is to train with a larger $b$ from the start, which lengthens every wavelength without a post-hoc surgery. The trajectory in deployed models is unambiguous: Llama 1 and 2 used $b=10^4$; Code Llama raised it to $10^6$ to reach 16k; Llama 3.1 uses $b = 5\times10^5$ with a 131{,}072-token window; Qwen2.5 uses $b=10^6$; the Qwen3.6 configs published this year use $b = 10^7$ with a native 262{,}144-token window, plus YaRN with factor 4 to reach roughly 1M. Verify Check any of these against the model's own config.json; the value moves between point releases.

ModelRoPE base $b$Native context
Llama 1 / 2$10^4$2k / 4k
Code Llama$10^6$16k
Llama 3.1$5\times10^5$131,072
Qwen2.5$10^6$131,072
Qwen3.6$10^7$262,144

What the base buys, in wavelength terms, is measurable. At $d_h = 128$ and $T_{\text{train}} = 8192$, the artifact reports the slowest wavelength $\lambda_{63}$ growing from $5.4\times10^4$ tokens at $b=10^4$ to $2.56\times10^6$ at $b=5\times10^5$ and $4.88\times10^7$ at $b=10^7$, with the number of pairs whose wavelength exceeds the trained context rising from 14 of 64 to 29 and then 35. That count is the tension: raising $b$ pushes more pairs into the never-completes-a-turn regime, where their contribution to the logit is a slowly varying, nearly monotone function of distance rather than a positional code. A very large base is therefore not free — it trades fine long-range positional resolution for the ability to define positions at all. Whether current bases are past the optimum is genuinely open. Men et al. (2024) derive a lower bound on $b$ from requiring the attention score to stay a decreasing function of distance: $8.4\times10^4$ for 8k, $7.8\times10^6$ for 128k. Verify Llama 3.1's $5\times10^5$ clears the 8k bound by six-fold and sits more than an order of magnitude below the bound for its own advertised 131k window — either the bound is loose, or a 131k window at $b=5\times10^5$ is a capacity claim rather than a retrieval claim. There is no matching upper bound with empirical support in either direction. Contested The evidence that would settle it is a controlled sweep of $b$ at fixed data and fixed target length, scored on retrieval at depth rather than perplexity; the published sweeps mostly vary two things at once.

19.7 Attention Sinks and Sliding Windows

Softmax is a probability distribution: the weights over the visible tokens must sum to one whether or not any of them is relevant. A trained model therefore needs somewhere to dump surplus mass, and it learns to use the first token — visible to every query under a causal mask, and, if it is a BOS token, semantically inert. This is the attention sink. In practice the first few tokens absorb a large, content-independent share of every head's attention.

The consequence is a real systems constraint. A sliding-window cache that keeps the last $W$ tokens and evicts everything else deletes the sink. The retained weights are $e_j/Z$ where $Z$ is the softmax denominator, so evicting tokens shrinks $Z$ and inflates every survivor by a common factor. The artifact measures this on 64 synthetic heads with $T=1024$, $W=128$, and a $+6$ sink logit: the window alone recovers only $0.0943$ of the full denominator $Z$, against $0.3373$ once the sink is added back. The $L_1$ error on the retained attention weights falls from $0.9057$ to $0.2532$ when the sink is kept, and the largest in-window weight is inflated $10.75\times$ over its true value when it is evicted. That inflation is the mechanism behind StreamingLLM's finding that perplexity explodes the moment the initial tokens leave the cache, and that keeping four of them plus a rolling window is enough to stream millions of tokens.

The field has since moved from patching this at inference to designing it away at training. gpt-oss adds a learnable per-head scalar to the softmax denominator, $\mathrm{softmax}_{\text{sink}}(x)_i = e^{x_i}/(\sum_j e^{x_j} + e^{\text{sink}_h})$, with the sink column discarded after normalization — one parameter per head, no KV entry, and the surplus mass now has a home that costs nothing to keep in a window. Verify The artifact's third variant models exactly this: a scalar in the denominator with no stored key or value recovers the window weights to $L_1$ error $0.2419$, marginally better than storing token 0's full KV pair, at zero cache cost. Explicit sinks are now standard rather than experimental; whether they eliminate the phenomenon or merely relocate it is still argued, since models with learned sinks still show outlier activations at early positions. Contested

19.8 What Long-Context Benchmarks Actually Measure

Needle-in-a-haystack — hide a sentence at depth $p$ in a long filler document, ask for it — measures verbatim single-fact retrieval under no distractor pressure. Frontier models saturate it, and saturation is now the standard argument that the benchmark is finished rather than that the problem is solved. RULER replaces it with 13 synthetic tasks in four families (retrieval, multi-hop tracing, aggregation, question answering) at controlled lengths, and defines effective context as the largest length at which a model stays above a threshold. Under that definition roughly half of the models tested at a claimed 32k failed to hold performance there. Verify

Two distinctions do most of the work. First, a claimed window is an architectural capacity statement — the model accepts the input — not a performance claim. Second, single-needle scores overstate multi-needle performance substantially, because integrating several facts requires the attention distribution to remain sharp at several depths simultaneously, which is exactly what the entropy growth in Section 19.5's temperature correction is fighting. Report effective context at a stated threshold on a multi-needle or aggregation task, and treat perplexity-at-length as a null result: ALiBi shows you can have flat perplexity and no retrieval.

Artifact 19.1 — RoPE Two Ways, and the Wavelength Ledger

Pure NumPy. Implements RoPE by complex multiplication and by explicit $2\times2$ real blocks, asserts they agree, asserts the relative-position property over 4000 random $(q,k,\Delta)$ at absolute positions up to $10^6$, then prints the per-pair wavelength table that shows exactly which dimensions PI, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN touch. torch appears only as an optional cross-check.

"""
Artifact 19.1 -- Rotary position embedding two independent ways, plus PI / NTK-aware /
YaRN reduced to one question: which frequency bands get their angular velocity divided
by the scale factor s?  Core is pure NumPy float64; torch is an optional cross-check.

Frequencies: theta_i = base ** (-2i/d_h), i = 0..d_h/2-1.  theta_0 = 1 (wavelength
2*pi tokens, fastest); theta_{d_h/2-1} ~ 1/base (slowest).  Wavelength lam_i = 2*pi/theta_i.
"Interleaved" pairing (RoFormer): coord 2i with 2i+1.  "Half-split" (GPT-NeoX/Llama):
coord j with j+d_h/2.  Same operator up to a fixed permutation -- checked below.
"""
import numpy as np
try:
    import torch
except ImportError:
    torch = None


# --- frequencies -------------------------------------------------------------------
def rope_freqs(d_h, base=10000.0):
    """theta_i = base**(-2i/d_h), radians per token, shape (d_h//2,)."""
    return base ** (-2.0 * np.arange(d_h // 2, dtype=np.float64) / d_h)


def wavelengths(theta):
    """lam_i = 2*pi/theta_i -- tokens per full rotation of coordinate pair i."""
    return 2.0 * np.pi / theta


# --- RoPE, implementation A: complex multiply --------------------------------------
def rope_complex(x, pos, theta):
    """z_i = x[2i] + j*x[2i+1]; multiply by exp(j*m*theta_i). x:(...,d_h) pos:(...)"""
    z = (x[..., 0::2] + 1j * x[..., 1::2]) * np.exp(1j * (pos[..., None] * theta))
    out = np.empty_like(x)
    out[..., 0::2], out[..., 1::2] = z.real, z.imag
    return out


# --- RoPE, implementation B: real 2x2 blocks ---------------------------------------
def rope_real_pairs(x, pos, theta):
    """Explicit [[c,-s],[s,c]] on each interleaved pair. No complex arithmetic."""
    ang = pos[..., None] * theta
    c, s = np.cos(ang), np.sin(ang)
    a, b = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]
    out = np.empty_like(x)
    out[..., 0::2], out[..., 1::2] = a * c - b * s, a * s + b * c
    return out


def rope_half_split(x, pos, theta):
    """GPT-NeoX / Llama "rotate_half" layout: coordinate j pairs with j + d_h/2."""
    h = x.shape[-1] // 2
    ang = pos[..., None] * theta
    c, s = np.cos(ang), np.sin(ang)
    a, b = x[..., :h], x[..., h:]
    return np.concatenate([a * c - b * s, a * s + b * c], axis=-1)


def perm(x):
    """P: interleaved coord 2i -> j=i, coord 2i+1 -> j=i+d_h/2."""
    return np.concatenate([x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]], axis=-1)


# --- context extension: each returns a modified frequency vector -------------------
def freqs_pi(theta, s):
    """Position interpolation (Chen et al. 2023): m -> m/s, every theta divided by s."""
    return theta / s


def freqs_ntk(d_h, base, s):
    """NTK-aware: base' = base * s**(d_h/(d_h-2)). Fastest pair fixed, slowest /s."""
    return rope_freqs(d_h, base * s ** (d_h / (d_h - 2.0)))


def yarn_ramp(r, alpha=1.0, beta=32.0):
    """gamma(r) = 0 for r<alpha, 1 for r>beta, linear between. r = L/lambda."""
    return np.clip((r - alpha) / (beta - alpha), 0.0, 1.0)


def freqs_yarn(theta, s, L, alpha=1.0, beta=32.0):
    """
    YaRN "NTK-by-parts": theta'_i = (1-g_i)*theta_i/s + g_i*theta_i, g_i = ramp(L/lam_i).
    r < alpha (pair never completes a rotation in training) -> fully interpolated.
    r > beta  (pair completes >= beta rotations)            -> left exactly alone.
    """
    g = yarn_ramp(L / wavelengths(theta), alpha, beta)
    return (1.0 - g) * (theta / s) + g * theta


def yarn_logit_scale(s):
    """YaRN attention temperature: logits multiplied by sqrt(1/t) = 0.1*ln(s) + 1."""
    return 0.1 * np.log(s) + 1.0


# --- checks -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def check_implementations(rng, d_h=128, base=10000.0):
    theta = rope_freqs(d_h, base)
    x = rng.standard_normal((512, d_h))
    pos = rng.integers(0, 200000, size=512).astype(np.float64)
    a, b = rope_complex(x, pos, theta), rope_real_pairs(x, pos, theta)
    print(f"  complex vs real-pair rotation, max |diff| = {np.max(np.abs(a - b)):.3e}")
    assert np.max(np.abs(a - b)) < 1e-7
    dn = np.max(np.abs(np.linalg.norm(a, axis=-1) - np.linalg.norm(x, axis=-1)))
    print(f"  ||R_m q|| - ||q||, max |diff|             = {dn:.3e}")
    assert dn < 1e-9
    c = rope_half_split(perm(x), pos, theta)
    print(f"  half-split(Px) vs P(interleaved x)        = {np.max(np.abs(c-perm(a))):.3e}")
    assert np.max(np.abs(c - perm(a))) < 1e-7
    return theta


def check_relative(rng, theta, d_h=128, n_trials=4000):
    """<R_m q, R_n k> must depend on m-n only: fix (q,k,delta), vary absolute (m,n)."""
    offsets = np.array([0, 1, 7, 113, 4096, 65536, 1_000_000], dtype=np.float64)
    worst = 0.0
    for _ in range(n_trials):
        q, k = rng.standard_normal(d_h), rng.standard_normal(d_h)
        delta = float(rng.integers(-8192, 8192))
        m = offsets + max(0.0, -delta)
        qm = rope_complex(np.broadcast_to(q, (m.size, d_h)), m, theta)
        kn = rope_complex(np.broadcast_to(k, (m.size, d_h)), m - delta, theta)
        v = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", qm, kn)
        worst = max(worst, float(v.max() - v.min()))
    print(f"  {n_trials} trials x {offsets.size} absolute positions (up to 1e6)")
    print(f"  max spread of <R_m q, R_n k> at fixed m-n = {worst:.3e}")
    assert worst < 1e-8, worst
    # The same test in float32: m*theta_i is formed before sin/cos, so a large absolute
    # position eats the low bits of the phase and the invariance degrades.
    for dt, tag in [(np.float64, "float64"), (np.float32, "float32")]:
        th = theta.astype(dt)
        q, k = (rng.standard_normal(d_h).astype(dt) for _ in range(2))
        m = np.array([0.0, 4096.0, 131072.0, 1048576.0], dtype=dt)
        qm = rope_real_pairs(np.broadcast_to(q, (4, d_h)).copy(), m, th)
        kn = rope_real_pairs(np.broadcast_to(k, (4, d_h)).copy(), m - dt(1000.0), th)
        v = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", qm, kn).astype(np.float64)
        print(f"  {tag} spread at m-n=1000, m in (0,4k,128k,1M) = {v.max()-v.min():.3e}")


def check_closed_form(rng, theta, d_h=128):
    """<R_m q,R_n k> = sum_i [A_i cos((m-n)th_i) - B_i sin((m-n)th_i)], A=qk pair dot,
    B = q_{2i+1}k_{2i} - q_{2i}k_{2i+1}. Only m-n appears on the right."""
    q, k = rng.standard_normal(d_h), rng.standard_normal(d_h)
    m, n = 9001.0, 137.0
    lhs = float(rope_complex(q, np.array(m), theta) @ rope_complex(k, np.array(n), theta))
    A = q[0::2] * k[0::2] + q[1::2] * k[1::2]
    B = q[1::2] * k[0::2] - q[0::2] * k[1::2]
    rhs = float(np.sum(A * np.cos((m - n) * theta) - B * np.sin((m - n) * theta)))
    print(f"  numeric {lhs:+.10f}  closed form {rhs:+.10f}  |diff| {abs(lhs-rhs):.3e}")
    assert abs(lhs - rhs) / abs(lhs) < 1e-12


def check_torch(rng, theta, d_h=128):
    if torch is None:
        print("  [skipped: torch not installed]")
        return
    x = rng.standard_normal((64, d_h))
    pos = rng.integers(0, 50000, size=64).astype(np.float64)
    ang = torch.from_numpy(pos)[:, None] * torch.from_numpy(theta)
    z = torch.view_as_complex(torch.from_numpy(x).reshape(64, d_h // 2, 2).contiguous())
    out = torch.view_as_real(z * torch.polar(torch.ones_like(ang), ang)).reshape(64, d_h)
    res = np.max(np.abs(out.numpy() - rope_complex(x, pos, theta)))
    print(f"  torch.view_as_complex path vs NumPy, max |diff| = {res:.3e}")
    assert res < 1e-9


def wavelength_table(d_h=128, base=10000.0, L=4096.0, s=8.0):
    theta = rope_freqs(d_h, base)
    lam, r = wavelengths(theta), L / wavelengths(theta)
    pi_, ntk, yarn, g = (freqs_pi(theta, s), freqs_ntk(d_h, base, s),
                         freqs_yarn(theta, s, L), yarn_ramp(L / wavelengths(theta)))
    assert abs(ntk[0] / theta[0] - 1.0) < 1e-12          # fastest pair untouched
    assert abs(ntk[-1] / theta[-1] - 1.0 / s) < 1e-12    # slowest pair == PI exactly
    assert np.all(yarn <= theta * (1 + 1e-12)) and np.all(yarn >= theta / s - 1e-18)
    print(f"  d_h={d_h} base={base:g} trained L={L:g} s={s:g} -> target {L*s:g} tokens; "
          f"YaRN alpha=1 beta=32, logit scale {yarn_logit_scale(s):.4f}")
    print("                                    theta'_i / theta_i")
    hdr = "  pair   lambda_i(tok)     r=L/lam      PI     NTK    YaRN   gamma"
    print(hdr + "\n  " + "-" * (len(hdr) - 2))
    for i in [0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 21, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 45, 46, 48, 52, 56, 60, 63]:
        print(f"  {i:4d} {lam[i]:15.2f} {r[i]:11.4f}  {pi_[i]/theta[i]:6.4f}  "
              f"{ntk[i]/theta[i]:6.4f}  {yarn[i]/theta[i]:6.4f}  {g[i]:5.3f}")
    hi, lo = int(np.sum(g >= 1 - 1e-12)), int(np.sum(g <= 1e-12))
    print(f"\n  PI       : all {d_h//2} pairs scaled by 1/s -- including the {hi} "
          f"short-wavelength pairs that never needed it")
    print(f"  NTK-aware: smooth sweep, pair 0 ratio {ntk[0]/theta[0]:.4f} -> pair "
          f"{d_h//2-1} ratio {ntk[-1]/theta[-1]:.4f} (= 1/s exactly)")
    print(f"  YaRN     : {hi} pairs untouched (r>32), {d_h//2-hi-lo} ramped, "
          f"{lo} fully interpolated (r<1)")
    print(f"  YaRN boundaries: last untouched pair i={hi-1} (lam={lam[hi-1]:.1f}); first "
          f"fully-interpolated pair i={d_h//2-lo} (lam={lam[d_h//2-lo]:.1f})")
    print(f"  {lo} of {d_h//2} pairs have lam > L, so positions in [{L:g},{L*s:g}) turn "
          f"them through angles never seen in training")


def base_table(d_h=128, L=8192.0):
    print(f"  d_h={d_h}; 'pairs with lam>L' at L={L:g}")
    print("  base           lam_max (tokens)   pairs with lam>L")
    for b in [1e4, 5e5, 1e6, 1e7]:
        lam = wavelengths(rope_freqs(d_h, b))
        print(f"  {b:>10.0f}   {lam[-1]:15.1f}   {int(np.sum(lam > L)):>10d} / {d_h//2}")


def sink_demo(rng, n=1024, d_h=64, window=128, sink_logit=6.0, trials=64):
    """
    Why the first KV pair must survive eviction. Token 0 carries a large content-
    independent logit and absorbs surplus softmax mass. Weights on the window are
    e_j/Z; dropping tokens shrinks Z and inflates every survivor.
    """
    theta = rope_freqs(d_h, 10000.0)
    pos = np.arange(n, dtype=np.float64)
    w = np.arange(n - window, n)
    ee, ek, eg, sm, ze, zk, mf, me = ([] for _ in range(8))
    for _ in range(trials):
        q = rng.standard_normal(d_h) / np.sqrt(d_h)
        k = rng.standard_normal((n, d_h)) / np.sqrt(d_h)
        kr = rope_real_pairs(k, pos, theta)
        qr = rope_real_pairs(q[None, :], np.array([float(n - 1)]), theta)[0]
        logits = kr @ qr * np.sqrt(d_h)
        logits[0] += sink_logit                       # the learned sink
        e = np.exp(logits - logits.max())
        Z, a_full = e.sum(), e / e.sum()
        Ze = e[w].sum()                               # window only
        Zk = e[w].sum() + e[0]                        # sink + window (StreamingLLM)
        Zg = e[w].sum() + np.exp(sink_logit - logits.max())   # gpt-oss: scalar, no KV
        ee.append(np.abs(e[w] / Ze - a_full[w]).sum())
        ek.append(np.abs(e[w] / Zk - a_full[w]).sum())
        eg.append(np.abs(e[w] / Zg - a_full[w]).sum())
        sm.append(a_full[0]); ze.append(Ze / Z); zk.append(Zk / Z)
        mf.append(a_full[w].max()); me.append((e[w] / Ze).max())
    print(f"  n={n}, window={window}, sink logit bonus +{sink_logit:g}, {trials} heads")
    print(f"  mean attention mass on token 0 (full context) : {np.mean(sm):.4f}")
    print(f"  denominator recovered, window only            : {np.mean(ze):.4f} of Z")
    print(f"  denominator recovered, sink + window          : {np.mean(zk):.4f} of Z")
    print(f"  L1 error on window weights, sink EVICTED      : {np.mean(ee):.4f}")
    print(f"  L1 error on window weights, sink KEPT         : {np.mean(ek):.4f}")
    print(f"  L1 error, learned scalar sink (no KV stored)  : {np.mean(eg):.4f}")
    print(f"  largest window weight: true {np.mean(mf):.4f} -> evicted "
          f"{np.mean(me):.4f} ({np.mean(me)/np.mean(mf):.2f}x inflated)")
    assert np.mean(ek) < np.mean(ee) and np.mean(eg) < np.mean(ee)


def head(t):
    print("\n" + "=" * 78 + f"\n{t}\n" + "=" * 78)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    head("[1] Two independent RoPE implementations agree")
    theta = check_implementations(rng)
    head("[2] <R_m q, R_n k> depends on m-n alone")
    check_relative(rng, theta)
    head("[3] Closed form of the rotated inner product")
    check_closed_form(rng, theta)
    head("[4] torch cross-check")
    check_torch(rng, theta)
    head("[5] Per-dimension wavelengths: who gets interpolated")
    wavelength_table()
    head("[6] Raising the base instead of interpolating")
    base_table()
    head("[7] Attention sink under a sliding window")
    sink_demo(rng)
    print("\nall assertions passed")

Running it takes about 1.9 s. The two implementations agree to $4.4\times10^{-16}$ and the half-split layout matches the interleaved one under the permutation to the same tolerance. Over 4000 trials at seven absolute positions each, the largest spread in $\langle R_m q, R_n k\rangle$ at fixed $m-n$ is $7.7\times10^{-10}$ against inner products of magnitude up to $47$ — translation invariance holds to float64 rounding out to position $10^6$. The wavelength table partitions the 64 pairs at $d_h=128$, $b=10^4$, $T_{\text{train}}=4096$, $s=8$ into 21 that YaRN leaves untouched, 25 ramped and 18 fully interpolated, against PI's uniform $0.1250$ ratio on all 64, and confirms NTK-aware scaling hits ratio $1.0000$ at pair 0 and exactly $0.1250$ at pair 63. The sink experiment ends with the line all assertions passed.

Key Takeaways
  • Attention is permutation-equivariant; the causal mask supplies an ordering but no metric, so position must be injected at the input, the logit, or the $q$–$k$ product. Certain
  • Any continuous, norm-preserving linear position map whose inner product depends only on $n-m$ is a set of $2\times2$ rotations in some basis. RoPE is not one option among many — it is the general solution, and the only free choice is the frequencies. Certain
  • PI, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN differ only in which pairs get $\theta_i \mapsto \theta_i/s$: all of them, a geometric sweep, or exactly those with rotation count $r_i = T_{\text{train}}/\lambda_i$ below $\alpha=1$, ramping to untouched above $\beta=32$. Certain
  • Deployed base frequencies have moved from $10^4$ to $5\times10^5$ (Llama 3.1) and $10^7$ (Qwen3.6); read the value from the checkpoint's config rather than from any book, including this one. Verify
  • The first token absorbs surplus softmax mass; evicting it shrinks the denominator and inflates every surviving weight (measured: $10.75\times$ on the largest). Current models replace the improvised sink with a learned per-head scalar in the denominator that needs no KV entry. Verify
Chapter 20

Vision Transformers and Multimodal Encoders

Learning Objectives
  • Derive patch embedding as a convolution whose kernel equals its stride, and compute the sequence length, parameter count and FLOPs of a base-size Vision Transformer at $224\times224$.
  • Explain why Vision Transformers lose to convolutional networks below roughly ten million images, and how augmentation, distillation and masked pretraining close the gap.
  • Derive the contrastive image–text objective, explain what the temperature $\tau$ controls, and derive the sigmoid-loss alternative and why it removes the all-gather dependence on batch size.
  • Explain self-distillation with an exponential-moving-average teacher, the roles of centering and sharpening, and why representational collapse is the failure mode to guard against.
  • Implement a Vision Transformer forward pass and both contrastive objectives in working code, verified against analytic parameter and FLOP formulas and by finite differences.
Read alongside — Prince, Understanding Deep Learning, for the clearest pictures of patch tokenization and of what a windowed attention map covers. Géron, Hands-On Machine Learning (2025 PyTorch edition), for image pipelines, augmentation stacks, and fine-tuning a pretrained backbone without breaking it. The primary papers are unusually readable: Dosovitskiy (ViT), Touvron (DeiT), Radford (CLIP), Zhai (sigmoid loss).

An image is a grid of pixels; a transformer eats a sequence of vectors. Everything here follows from how you convert one into the other, and from the fact that the conversion Dosovitskiy et al. chose in 2020 — cut the image into $16\times16$ tiles, flatten, project — discards almost every structural assumption Chapter 16 spent a chapter defending. The Vision Transformer has no translation equivariance, no locality prior, no multi-scale hierarchy. It loses badly at ImageNet scale and wins decisively at three hundred million images. That is the whole argument, and it generalizes: a weak inductive bias plus enough data beats a strong one. Sections 20.1–20.2 build the architecture and price it; 20.3 confronts the data hunger; 20.4–20.6 are about the objective, where the progress since 2021 has actually happened; 20.8 connects the encoder to Part V's language models.

20.1 Images as Token Sequences

Let $x \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}$ be an image, where $C$ is the channel count — the one place in this book $C$ does not mean compute in FLOPs. Choose $P$ dividing $H$ and $W$ and cut $x$ into $n_p = HW/P^2$ non-overlapping tiles, each in $\mathbb{R}^{C\times P\times P}$.

Definition 20.1 (Patch embedding)

The patch embedding is the affine map $z_i = E\,\mathrm{vec}(x_i) + b$ with $E \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times CP^2}$, applied to every tile. Equivalently it is one convolution with kernel $P$, stride $P$, $C$ input and $d$ output channels: stride equal to kernel makes the receptive fields tile the image without overlap, and the resulting $d\times(H/P)\times(W/P)$ feature map, flattened over space, is the token sequence. The artifact verifies this against conv2d to $7.8\times10^{-16}$.

The equivalence locates exactly how much convolutional prior survives: one layer, receptive field $16\times16$, no overlap, after which every operation is permutation-equivariant global attention. It also makes patch size a re-parameterization rather than an architecture change — FlexiViT and NaFlex exploit this by resizing $E$ itself.

A learned class token $z_{\text{cls}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is prepended, and a learned position embedding $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ with $n = n_p + 1$ is added. Both are necessary for the same reason given in Chapter 18: self-attention is permutation-equivariant, so without $p$ the model literally cannot tell a face from its scrambled tiles. Factorized 2-D row/column embeddings do not help; learned 1-D embeddings recover the grid topology on their own.

Example 20.1 (Sequence length at standard resolution)

At $H=W=224$, $P=16$: $n_p = (224/16)^2 = 14^2 = 196$ patches, so $n = 197$ tokens. Each token is a flattened $3\times16\times16 = 768$-dimensional tile, numerically equal to $d$ for ViT-Base by coincidence of the constants. At $P=14$ the same image gives $256$ patches; at $448$ with $P=16$ it gives $784$, and since attention is quadratic in $n$, doubling the side length multiplies the attention term by sixteen.

20.2 The ViT Architecture and Its Costs

After embedding, the model is $L$ pre-norm transformer blocks exactly as derived in Section 18.5 — GELU feed-forward, no causal mask — then a final LayerNorm and a linear head reading the class token. Nothing is vision-specific after the first layer.

Parameters. With MLP ratio $4$ and biases everywhere, a block holds $3d^2+3d$ (fused QKV), $d^2+d$ (projection), $4d^2+4d$ and $4d^2+d$ (MLP), $4d$ (two LayerNorms):

$$N_{\text{block}} = 12d^2 + 13d, \qquad N = \underbrace{(CP^2+1)d}_{\text{patch embed}} + \underbrace{d}_{\text{cls}} + \underbrace{nd}_{\text{pos}} + L\,(12d^2+13d) + \underbrace{2d}_{\text{final LN}} .$$
Example 20.2 (ViT-Base/16 parameter count)

$d=768$, $L=12$, $n=197$. Patch embed $= 769\times768 = 590{,}592$. Position $= 197\times768 = 151{,}296$. Per block $= 12(768)^2 + 13(768) = 7{,}077{,}888 + 9{,}984 = 7{,}087{,}872$, so twelve blocks give $85{,}054{,}464$. Summing with the class token and the final LayerNorm: $85{,}798{,}656$ backbone parameters. A 1000-way ImageNet head adds $768{,}000 + 1000$, for $86{,}567{,}656$ — the "86M" everyone quotes. The artifact asserts this exact integer. Certain

FLOPs. Counting multiply-accumulates for one image and ignoring the $O(nd)$ elementwise work in LayerNorm, GELU and softmax, each block costs $12nd^2$ for the four projections plus two MLP matmuls, and $2n^2d$ for $QK^\top$ and $AV$:

$$\mathrm{MACs} = n_p\,CP^2 d \;+\; L\big(12nd^2 + 2n^2d\big) \;+\; d\,n_{\text{cls}} .$$

For ViT-Base/16 at $224$ this evaluates to $1.756\times10^{10}$ MACs, i.e. $17.56$ G — the artifact prints the exact integer $17{,}563{,}828{,}224$. Published tables quoting "$17.6$ GFLOPs" for ViT-B/16 are counting MACs; under the two-FLOPs-per-MAC convention used elsewhere in this book the figure is $35.1$ GFLOPs. Check the convention before comparing tables across papers. Certain

Theorem 20.1 (Where attention starts to dominate)

The quadratic term $2n^2d$ equals the linear term $12nd^2$ at $n = 6d$.

Proof. $2n^2d = 12nd^2 \iff n = 6d$. $\blacksquare$

For $d=768$ that is $4608$ tokens. At $n=197$ attention matmuls are $4.10\%$ of a block's arithmetic (measured in the artifact), so ViT-Base at standard resolution is overwhelmingly dense matrix multiplies and FlashAttention (Chapter 31) buys it almost nothing. The picture inverts for high-resolution or video input: a $1088\times1088$ image at $P=16$ already gives $68^2 = 4624$ patches, just past the crossover.

Model$d$$L$headsParams (P=16, no head)
ViT-Small38412621.7 M
ViT-Base768121285.8 M
ViT-Large10242416303.3 M
ViT-Huge12803216630.9 M

These follow from the formula above. Every model in Sections 20.5–20.8 is one of these four shapes or a mild variant — SigLIP's So400m is a compute-optimal shape found by search rather than a round number. Certain

20.3 Data Hunger, DeiT, and Distillation

Trained on ImageNet-1k alone, ViT-Base reaches roughly $77\%$ top-1 — several points below a ResNet of comparable cost. On ImageNet-21k it draws level; on JFT-300M it wins clearly. The controlled experiment used random JFT subsets of 9M, 30M and 90M plus the full 300M: BiT ResNets dominate the small subsets, the curves cross between 30M and 100M, ViT is ahead at 300M. Likely (the crossover moves with model size and augmentation, so "roughly ten million" is an order of magnitude, not a threshold).

The mechanism is Chapter 3's bias–variance story made concrete. A convolution is a linear map constrained to be translation-equivariant and local — a hard restriction of the hypothesis class that happens to be true of natural images. Attention over patches strictly contains that class, so a ViT can represent any convolution but must identify locality from data instead of being handed it, and identification costs samples. Below the crossover the constraint is worth more than the extra capacity; above it, the constraint is a ceiling. Three families of fixes emerged, and they stack.

Augmentation and regularization. DeiT trains ViT-Base to $81.8\%$ on ImageNet-1k alone given RandAugment, Mixup, CutMix, random erasing, stochastic depth, repeated augmentation and a long schedule. The architecture did not change: "ViT needs 300M images" was always a claim about a recipe. Certain

Distillation from a convolutional teacher. DeiT adds a distillation token, symmetric with the class token, trained to match a teacher's prediction. Hard distillation (cross-entropy against the teacher's $\arg\max$) beat soft (KL against a softened distribution), and a convnet teacher beat a transformer teacher of equal accuracy. That second fact is the interesting one: the student inherits the teacher's inductive bias through its labels, which is exactly the missing ingredient. DeiT-B rises from $81.8\%$ to $83.4\%$. Verify against the DeiT paper; numbers shift by tenths across schedules.

Reintroducing bias into the architecture — convolutional stems, overlapping patches, hierarchical stages (Section 20.7). This works, and concedes that the pure-ViT position was overstated for small data.

Common Pitfall

Fine-tuning a pretrained ViT at a higher resolution changes $n_p$, so the learned position embedding no longer matches the sequence. The fix is to bilinearly interpolate the $\sqrt{n_p}\times\sqrt{n_p}$ grid of position vectors — but the table has $n_p+1$ rows and row 0 belongs to the class token, which has no spatial location. Interpolating all rows as if they formed a grid smears the class-token embedding into its neighbours. The model still trains and accuracy degrades rather than collapses, which is why the bug survives review. Likely Slice off row 0, interpolate rows $1{:}$, concatenate.

20.4 Masked Image Modeling

Chapter 23's lesson is that a self-supervised reconstruction objective converts unlabeled data into representation. BEiT transplanted it by discretizing patches with a learned tokenizer and predicting token indices — effective, but it adds a training stage. MAE dropped the tokenizer, regressed raw pixels, and made two choices that carry the method:

A very high mask ratio. MAE masks $75\%$ of patches against BERT's $15\%$. Images are far more redundant than text: at $15\%$ a patch is recoverable by local interpolation, so the model learns a denoiser rather than a representation. At $75\%$ the task requires knowing what objects are. Certain

An asymmetric encoder–decoder. The encoder sees only the $25\%$ visible patches — mask tokens are not fed to it at all — and a shallow decoder receives the encoded visible tokens plus mask tokens and reconstructs pixels. Since encoder cost is near-linear in token count at these lengths (Theorem 20.1), a quarter of the sequence cuts encoder FLOPs about fourfold, which is what makes the $\ge 3\times$ end-to-end speedup possible. The decoder is discarded afterwards. A vanilla ViT-Huge pretrained this way reaches $87.8\%$ top-1 among ImageNet-1k-only methods. Verify (MAE paper, ViT-H fine-tuned at $448$).

The caveat: MAE features are excellent under full fine-tuning and weak under linear probing, because pixel reconstruction preserves low-level information a linear head cannot ignore. Contrastive and self-distillation objectives invert that ranking, which decides the choice whenever the backbone stays frozen. Likely

20.5 Contrastive Vision–Language: CLIP

CLIP stopped predicting labels and started predicting which caption goes with which image, over 400M web pairs. A vision encoder $f$ and a text encoder $g$ map into a shared $\mathbb{R}^{m}$, both $\ell_2$-normalized so similarity is a cosine.

Definition 20.2 (Symmetric InfoNCE / contrastive image–text loss)

For a batch of $B$ matched pairs, let $u_i = f(x_i)/\lVert f(x_i)\rVert$, $v_j = g(y_j)/\lVert g(y_j)\rVert$, and $M_{ij} = u_i^\top v_j/\tau$. With $P^{\text{row}} = \mathrm{softmax}(M)$ over $j$ and $P^{\text{col}} = \mathrm{softmax}(M)$ over $i$, $$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\Big(\log P^{\text{row}}_{ii} + \log P^{\text{col}}_{ii}\Big).$$ The $B$ diagonal entries are positives; all $B^2-B$ off-diagonal entries are negatives, obtained free from the batch. The gradient with respect to the logits is $$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial M} = \frac{1}{2B}\Big[(P^{\text{row}} - I) + (P^{\text{col}} - I)\Big],$$ which is the standard "predicted minus target" form of Chapter 2 applied twice.

What $\tau$ does. Cosine similarities live in $[-1,1]$, so without $1/\tau$ the softmax over $B$ items is nearly uniform and the gradient signal is tiny. It sets how sharply the loss concentrates on hard negatives: as $\tau \to 0$ the row distribution collapses onto the single most similar negative and InfoNCE approaches a max-margin objective; as $\tau \to \infty$ all negatives weigh equally. The artifact measures this on eight random pairs: mean row entropy falls from $1.9946$ nats at $\tau=1$ (uniform is $\log 8 = 2.0794$) to $0.4429$ at $\tau=0.07$ and $0.0089$ at $\tau=0.01$, the largest off-diagonal weight rising from $0.237$ to $0.986$. CLIP learns $\log(1/\tau)$ from $\tau=0.07$ and clamps $1/\tau \le 100$; without the clamp the optimizer drives $\tau\to 0$, because sharpening the softmax lowers the loss faster than improving representations does, and training destabilizes. Certain

The softmax normalizer has two consequences. The loss depends on the whole batch, so more negatives means a better estimate of the partition function — CLIP used batch $32{,}768$. And data-parallel training needs an all-gather: no row's normalizer is known until every device's embeddings are present, and the $B\times B$ logit matrix is materialized somewhere.

20.5.1 SigLIP and the Sigmoid Loss
Definition 20.3 (Pairwise sigmoid loss)

Let $z_{ij} = +1$ if $i=j$ and $-1$ otherwise, and let $a_{ij} = t'\,u_i^\top v_j + b$ with learnable scale $t' > 0$ and bias $b$. Then $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{sig}} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{j=1}^{B} -\log \sigma\!\big(z_{ij}\,a_{ij}\big), \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{sig}}}{\partial a_{ij}} = -\frac{z_{ij}\,\sigma(-z_{ij}a_{ij})}{B}.$$ Every pair is an independent binary classification: matched or not. The bias $b$ starts strongly negative (SigLIP uses $-10$) because $B^2-B$ of the $B^2$ terms are negatives; without it the first steps just push everything apart.

Theorem 20.2 (The sigmoid loss decomposes over pairs; InfoNCE does not)

$\mathcal{L}_{\text{sig}} = \sum_{i,j} \ell(u_i, v_j)$ for a function $\ell$ of one image embedding and one text embedding. Hence for $j \neq k$, $\;\partial^2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{sig}}/\partial v_j\,\partial v_k = 0$. For InfoNCE the same mixed derivative is nonzero.

Proof. Each term of $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sig}}$ contains exactly one $u$ and one $v$, so no term contains both $v_j$ and $v_k$; differentiating a sum of such terms twice in two distinct $v$'s annihilates every term. For InfoNCE, $\log P^{\text{row}}_{ii} = M_{ii} - \log\sum_{j}e^{M_{ij}}$, and the log-sum-exp couples all $v_j$ within row $i$. Writing $p = P^{\text{row}}_{i\cdot}$, its second derivative in the $v$'s is $\tau^{-2}\big(\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^\top\big)_{jk}\,u_iu_i^\top$, whose $j\neq k$ entry is $-\tau^{-2}p_jp_k\,u_iu_i^\top \neq 0$. $\blacksquare$

The artifact measures both: perturbing text embedding 3 changes the gradient at text embedding 5 by $7.62\times10^{-2}$ under InfoNCE and by exactly $0$ under the sigmoid loss.

That is the systems argument. Because loss and gradient are additive over pairs, a device computes the complete contribution of its own $b\times b$ block and adds it in; no cross-device reduction precedes the arithmetic. The standard implementation passes text chunks around a ring so each device sees every text block in turn, with $O(b^2)$ memory instead of $O(B^2)$ and no all-gather. The artifact shows the decomposition directly: accumulating the sigmoid loss over $2\times2$ blocks of pairs reproduces the full value $10.146099686362$ to a difference of exactly $0$, whereas the analogous block-local accumulation for InfoNCE gives $5.350409$ against a true $8.808721$ — an error of $3.46$, because renormalizing inside a chunk is a different loss.

The sigmoid loss also removes the pressure toward enormous batches: it beats softmax substantially below batch $16$k, and both saturate near $32$k — which reframes CLIP's giant batches as partly an artifact of the normalizer. Verify (SigLIP paper, Figure 2).

SigLIP 2 (2025) keeps the sigmoid loss and stacks objectives on top: a captioning decoder, self-distillation and masked prediction, online data curation, multilingual data. It ships at ViT-B (86M), L (303M), So400m (400M) and g (1B), and adds NaFlex variants that process images at native aspect ratio by resizing so both sides are multiples of the patch size and the sequence fits a target length, following NaViT and FlexiViT. Reach for NaFlex on documents and OCR, where squashing a page to a square destroys the glyphs. Verify (counts and available NaFlex sizes per the model card; the family gains checkpoints).

20.6 Self-Distillation: DINO and Its Successors

Contrastive learning needs pairs. Self-distillation needs only images: a student is trained to match a teacher that is a slowly-moving copy of itself.

Definition 20.4 (Self-distillation with an EMA teacher)

Student parameters $\theta_s$ and teacher parameters $\theta_t$ share an architecture. Two augmented views $x_1,x_2$ of one image are drawn; the loss is the cross-entropy $-P_t(x_2)^\top \log P_s(x_1)$, summed over view pairs, where $P_s = \mathrm{softmax}(h_s(x)/\tau_s)$ and $P_t = \mathrm{softmax}\big((h_t(x)-c)/\tau_t\big)$. Gradients flow only into $\theta_s$; the teacher is updated as $\theta_t \leftarrow \lambda\theta_t + (1-\lambda)\theta_s$ with $\lambda$ near $1$ (typically ramped $0.996 \to 1$), and the center as $c \leftarrow mc + (1-m)\,\mathbb{E}_{\text{batch}}[h_t(x)]$.

Nothing in that objective forbids the trivial solution: a constant output vector minimizes the loss. This is representational collapse: complete, where every input maps to one output, or dimensional, where outputs span a low-dimensional subspace. DINO's defense is a pair of opposed forces applied to the teacher only:

  • Centering subtracts a running mean from the teacher logits. It prevents any single output dimension from dominating — but on its own it pushes the teacher distribution toward uniform, which is collapse to a constant.
  • Sharpening uses a lower teacher temperature ($\tau_t \approx 0.04$ against $\tau_s = 0.1$). It prevents the uniform solution — but on its own it encourages one dimension to dominate.

Each measure causes exactly the failure the other prevents, and DINO's ablation is the argument: remove either and training collapses within a few thousand steps. The balance is empirical, not derived, and the stable region in $(\tau_t, \tau_s, m)$ is narrow. Contested Whether collapse prevention requires such hand-tuning is disputed: SwAV enforces equipartition via Sinkhorn–Knopp, VICReg adds variance and covariance penalties with no teacher, and BYOL claims a predictor plus stop-gradient suffices. What would settle it is a fixed-compute ablation across all four with augmentation held constant; published comparisons do not control augmentation, which alone moves linear-probe accuracy by several points.

DINO's striking result was that class-token attention maps segment objects with no segmentation label ever seen. DINOv2 scaled the recipe on a curated 142M-image corpus (LVD-142M), making frozen features competitive on dense tasks. DINOv3 (2025) scales again: a ViT-7B/16 of $6{,}716$M parameters on LVD-1689M, roughly 1.7 billion curated web images. Verify

Its new idea addresses a failure that appears only at that scale. Over long schedules the dense patch features degrade even as global benchmarks improve: patch-level consistency decays while the class-token representation dominates. Gram anchoring constrains not the patch features but their Gram matrix — all pairwise dot products between patch features — to stay near that of an earlier, stable "Gram teacher" checkpoint. Individual features may drift; their relative geometry may not. Applied late (after roughly 1M iterations, Gram teacher refreshed periodically), it restores dense-feature quality and lifts ADE20k segmentation at little cost to global metrics. The released family is a distillation ladder from the 7B teacher — ViT-S (21M), S+ (29M), B (86M), L (300M), H+ (840M), ConvNeXt from 29M to 198M — plus a ViT-7B trained on 493M satellite images. Verify (model card; sizes and dataset names are stable, counts are rounded).

20.7 Hierarchical and Windowed ViTs

Plain ViT produces one feature map at one scale. Detection and segmentation want a pyramid, at resolutions where $n=197$ is laughably small. Swin supplies both by returning some discarded structure: attention runs inside non-overlapping $M\times M$ windows, and patches merge between stages so resolution halves and width doubles, as in a convnet.

Global attention over $n$ tokens costs $2n^2d$ MACs; windowed attention over $n/M^2$ windows of $M^2$ tokens costs $(n/M^2)\cdot 2M^4 d = 2nM^2d$, linear in $n$. At $M=7$, $n=3136$ (a $224$ image at patch $4$), that is a $3136/49 = 64\times$ reduction.

Windows sever communication across their boundaries, so alternate blocks shift the grid by $\lfloor M/2 \rfloor$. The efficient implementation cyclically rolls the feature map and masks the wrapped-around entries rather than padding; forgetting that mask is a classic silent bug — the model trains, and the left edge attends to the right edge as if adjacent.

The verdict is mixed. Hierarchy is right for dense prediction, but ViTDet showed a plain ViT with a simple feature pyramid built from the last layer competes on detection when the backbone is pretrained well. Hierarchy buys efficiency and small-data performance, not accuracy. Likely

20.8 Feeding Vision to a Language Model

The dominant recipe: run a frozen or lightly-tuned vision encoder, project its patch tokens into the language model's embedding space, concatenate with text tokens. The projector is a two-layer MLP (LLaVA) or a small set of learned queries cross-attending to the patch grid (Q-Former, Perceiver resampler). The MLP preserves every patch; the resampler fixes the token budget, which matters because $196$ tokens at $224$ becomes $2{,}304$ for a $768\times768$ document, and tiling ("AnyRes") multiplies that again.

Which encoder to attach depends on the downstream task, because the dominant pretraining objectives produce complementary defects:

FamilyObjectiveStrong atWeak at
CLIP / SigLIP 2image–text contrastive (+ caption, self-distill)zero-shot classification, retrieval, VLM inputdense prediction, spatial precision
DINOv2 / DINOv3self-distillation (+ Gram anchoring)segmentation, depth, correspondencelanguage alignment
MAE / BEiTmasked reconstructionfine-tuning initializationfrozen linear probes

Meta's Perception Encoder (NeurIPS 2025) sharpened this: the best general-purpose visual embeddings are not at the output layer. PE trains one contrastive objective, and its intermediate layers rival AIMv2 for language tasks and DINOv2 for spatial tasks, while the final layer — the one the loss actually shapes — is poor for many uses. PE ships alignment tunings that surface the middle layers: PE-Lang for multimodal LLM input, PE-Spatial for dense prediction, via self-distillation and SAM2-based correspondence distillation. If you attach a CLIP-style encoder and read only its last hidden state, you are probably reading the wrong layer. Verify

The synthesis arrived in 2026: Meta's EUPE (Efficient Universal Perception Encoder) distills PE-Core, PE-Lang and DINOv3 into a single 1.9B "proxy teacher" whose latent space holds semantic and geometric features together, then distills that one teacher down to ViT-T/16 (6M), ViT-S/16 (21M), ViT-B/16 (86M) and ConvNeXt variants to 89M — all under 100M parameters, matching same-size specialists on all three task families. Scaling up before scaling down is the contribution; direct multi-teacher distillation into a small student works less well. Verify (arXiv 2603.22387, March 2026; benchmark claims are the authors' own, independent replication is not in yet.)

Note what has not changed since 2020. The architecture of Sections 20.1–20.2 — patch embedding, class token, pre-norm blocks — is the architecture of every model named above. What changed is the objective and the data: supervised classification to contrastive alignment to sigmoid alignment to self-distillation to multi-objective recipes and cross-teacher distillation. The frontier is the loss, not the network. Likely

Artifact 20.1 — ViT Forward Pass, InfoNCE, and the Sigmoid Loss

Part 1 builds a ViT in NumPy — patchify, class token, position embedding, pre-norm blocks with exact-erf GELU — and checks ViT-Base/16's parameter count against the closed form of Section 20.2, a tiny ViT's parameters against its constructed arrays, and its multiply-accumulates against the FLOP formula by instrumenting every matmul. Part 2 implements both objectives with hand-derived gradients (including the $\ell_2$-normalization Jacobian), verifies them by central finite differences, and demonstrates Theorem 20.2. No timm, no pretrained weights.

"""
Chapter 20 Artifact -- Vision Transformers and Multimodal Encoders.

Part 1: a ViT forward pass from scratch (patchify as a strided convolution,
        class token, position embedding, pre-norm blocks), with parameters and
        MACs checked against closed forms.  ViT-Base/16 is counted by shape; a
        tiny ViT is executed with every matmul instrumented.
Part 2: InfoNCE and the pairwise sigmoid loss from scratch, gradients verified
        by central finite differences, plus numerical evidence that InfoNCE
        couples the batch while the sigmoid loss decomposes over pairs.

No timm, no pretrained weights, no downloads.  torch is an optional cross-check.
"""

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import erf, expit  # expit == logistic sigmoid

try:
    import torch
except ImportError:  # pragma: no cover
    torch = None

RNG = np.random.default_rng(0)
_MACS = [0]  # instrumented multiply-accumulate counter


def mm(a, b):
    """Matmul that records its multiply-accumulate count."""
    _MACS[0] += a.shape[0] * a.shape[1] * b.shape[1]
    return a @ b


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Closed-form parameter and MAC counts
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
BASE = dict(img=224, patch=16, d=768, L=12, heads=12, ch=3, n_cls=1000)
TINY = dict(img=32, patch=8, d=48, L=3, heads=4, ch=3, n_cls=10)


def analytic_params(c):
    """Parameter count of a pre-norm ViT with MLP ratio 4, all biases present."""
    d, P, L = c["d"], c["patch"], c["L"]
    n_patch = (c["img"] // P) ** 2
    n = n_patch + 1                                  # + class token
    patch_embed = c["ch"] * P * P * d + d            # strided conv weight+bias
    # per block: qkv (3d^2+3d) + proj (d^2+d) + fc1 (4d^2+4d) + fc2 (4d^2+d)
    #            + two LayerNorms (4d)  =  12 d^2 + 13 d
    block = 12 * d * d + 13 * d
    return dict(
        n_patch=n_patch, n=n,
        patch_embed=patch_embed, cls=d, pos=n * d,
        blocks=L * block, final_ln=2 * d,
        backbone=patch_embed + d + n * d + L * block + 2 * d,
        head=d * c["n_cls"] + c["n_cls"],
    )


def analytic_macs(c):
    """Multiply-accumulates for one image, matmuls only (LN/softmax/GELU are O(nd))."""
    d, P, L = c["d"], c["patch"], c["L"]
    n_patch = (c["img"] // P) ** 2
    n = n_patch + 1
    pe = n_patch * (c["ch"] * P * P) * d              # patch projection
    # per block: 12 n d^2 (four projections + two MLP matmuls) + 2 n^2 d (QK^T, AV)
    blk = 12 * n * d * d + 2 * n * n * d
    return dict(patch_embed=pe, per_block=blk, blocks=L * blk,
                head=d * c["n_cls"], total=pe + L * blk + d * c["n_cls"])


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The model
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def init_vit(c, rng):
    d, P, L, ch = c["d"], c["patch"], c["L"], c["ch"]
    n = (c["img"] // P) ** 2 + 1
    s = 0.02
    p = {
        "pe_w": rng.normal(0, s, (d, ch * P * P)),   # == conv weight (d,ch,P,P)
        "pe_b": np.zeros(d),
        "cls": rng.normal(0, s, (1, d)),
        "pos": rng.normal(0, s, (n, d)),
        "ln_g": np.ones(d), "ln_b": np.zeros(d),
        "head_w": rng.normal(0, s, (c["n_cls"], d)), "head_b": np.zeros(c["n_cls"]),
        "blocks": [],
    }
    for _ in range(L):
        p["blocks"].append({
            "n1g": np.ones(d), "n1b": np.zeros(d),
            "qkv_w": rng.normal(0, s, (3 * d, d)), "qkv_b": np.zeros(3 * d),
            "pr_w": rng.normal(0, s, (d, d)), "pr_b": np.zeros(d),
            "n2g": np.ones(d), "n2b": np.zeros(d),
            "f1_w": rng.normal(0, s, (4 * d, d)), "f1_b": np.zeros(4 * d),
            "f2_w": rng.normal(0, s, (d, 4 * d)), "f2_b": np.zeros(d),
        })
    return p


def count_params(p):
    tot = sum(v.size for k, v in p.items() if k != "blocks")
    return tot + sum(a.size for blk in p["blocks"] for a in blk.values())


def patchify(x, W, b, P):
    """Patch embedding == convolution with kernel P and stride P. x: (ch,H,W)."""
    ch, H, Wd = x.shape
    t = x.reshape(ch, H // P, P, Wd // P, P).transpose(1, 3, 0, 2, 4)
    cols = t.reshape((H // P) * (Wd // P), ch * P * P)   # (n_patch, ch*P*P)
    return mm(cols, W.T) + b


def layernorm(x, g, b, eps=1e-5):
    mu = x.mean(-1, keepdims=True)
    var = x.var(-1, keepdims=True)
    return (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps) * g + b


def gelu(x):
    return 0.5 * x * (1.0 + erf(x / np.sqrt(2.0)))


def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = z - z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)


def mha(x, blk, heads):
    n, d = x.shape
    dh = d // heads
    qkv = mm(x, blk["qkv_w"].T) + blk["qkv_b"]
    q, k, v = np.split(qkv, 3, axis=1)
    out = np.empty_like(x)
    for h in range(heads):
        sl = slice(h * dh, (h + 1) * dh)
        a = softmax(mm(q[:, sl], k[:, sl].T) / np.sqrt(dh))
        out[:, sl] = mm(a, v[:, sl])
    return mm(out, blk["pr_w"].T) + blk["pr_b"]


def vit_forward(img, p, c):
    """Pre-norm ViT. img: (ch,H,W). Returns (logits, tokens)."""
    z = patchify(img, p["pe_w"], p["pe_b"], c["patch"])
    z = np.concatenate([p["cls"], z], axis=0) + p["pos"]
    for blk in p["blocks"]:
        z = z + mha(layernorm(z, blk["n1g"], blk["n1b"]), blk, c["heads"])
        h = layernorm(z, blk["n2g"], blk["n2b"])
        z = z + mm(gelu(mm(h, blk["f1_w"].T) + blk["f1_b"]), blk["f2_w"].T) + blk["f2_b"]
    z = layernorm(z, p["ln_g"], p["ln_b"])
    return mm(z[:1], p["head_w"].T) + p["head_b"], z


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Contrastive objectives
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def l2n(X):
    return X / np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1, keepdims=True)


def _unnorm_grad(X, G):
    """Push a gradient w.r.t. u = x/||x|| back through the normalization."""
    nrm = np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    U = X / nrm
    return (G - U * (G * U).sum(1, keepdims=True)) / nrm


def infonce(Xi, Xt, logit_scale):
    """Symmetric CLIP loss.  Returns (loss, dXi, dXt)."""
    B = Xi.shape[0]
    Zi, Zt = l2n(Xi), l2n(Xt)
    S = Zi @ Zt.T
    M = S * logit_scale
    Pr, Pc = softmax(M, axis=1), softmax(M, axis=0)
    I = np.eye(B)
    loss = -0.5 * (np.log(np.diag(Pr)).sum() + np.log(np.diag(Pc)).sum()) / B
    G = 0.5 / B * ((Pr - I) + (Pc - I))       # dL/dM
    dS = G * logit_scale
    return loss, _unnorm_grad(Xi, dS @ Zt), _unnorm_grad(Xt, dS.T @ Zi)


def siglip(Xi, Xt, logit_scale, bias):
    """Pairwise sigmoid loss.  Returns (loss, dXi, dXt)."""
    B = Xi.shape[0]
    Zi, Zt = l2n(Xi), l2n(Xt)
    S = Zi @ Zt.T
    Z = 2.0 * np.eye(B) - 1.0                 # +1 on the diagonal, -1 elsewhere
    A = logit_scale * S + bias
    loss = -np.log(expit(Z * A)).sum() / B
    dS = -(Z * expit(-Z * A)) * logit_scale / B
    return loss, _unnorm_grad(Xi, dS @ Zt), _unnorm_grad(Xt, dS.T @ Zi)


def fd_check(fn, Xi, Xt, rng, k=40, h=1e-5):
    """Central finite differences on k random coordinates of each input."""
    _, gi, gt = fn(Xi, Xt)
    worst = 0.0
    for side, g in ((0, gi), (1, gt)):
        for _ in range(k):
            i, j = int(rng.integers(g.shape[0])), int(rng.integers(g.shape[1]))
            A, Bm = Xi.copy(), Xt.copy()
            X = A if side == 0 else Bm
            X[i, j] += h; lp = fn(A, Bm)[0]
            X[i, j] -= 2 * h; lm = fn(A, Bm)[0]
            worst = max(worst, abs((lp - lm) / (2 * h) - g[i, j]))
    return worst


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.set_printoptions(precision=6, suppress=True)

    print("=" * 74)
    print("PART 1  ViT geometry, parameters, FLOPs")
    print("=" * 74)
    ab, mb = analytic_params(BASE), analytic_macs(BASE)
    print(f"ViT-Base/16 @224: patches={ab['n_patch']}  sequence length n={ab['n']}")
    print(f"  patch embed {ab['patch_embed']:>12,}   pos embed {ab['pos']:>12,}")
    print(f"  12 blocks   {ab['blocks']:>12,}   backbone  {ab['backbone']:>12,}")
    print(f"  + 1000-way head -> {ab['backbone'] + ab['head']:,} total")
    print(f"  MACs/image  {mb['total']:,}  = {mb['total']/1e9:.2f} G"
          f"   ({2*mb['total']/1e9:.2f} GFLOPs at 2 FLOPs per MAC)")
    quad = 2 * ab["n"] ** 2 * BASE["d"]
    print(f"  attention-matmul share of a block: {quad/mb['per_block']*100:.2f}%"
          f"   (2n^2 d = 12 n d^2 at n = 6d = {6*BASE['d']} tokens)")
    assert ab["backbone"] == 85_798_656 and ab["n"] == 197
    assert ab["backbone"] + ab["head"] == 86_567_656

    # exact parameter count by construction, tiny config
    p = init_vit(TINY, RNG)
    at = analytic_params(TINY)
    built = count_params(p)
    print(f"\ntiny ViT (d=48,L=3,32px/patch8): built={built:,} "
          f"analytic={at['backbone']+at['head']:,}  diff={built-(at['backbone']+at['head'])}")
    assert built == at["backbone"] + at["head"]

    # instrumented MAC count of a real forward pass vs the closed form
    img = RNG.normal(size=(TINY["ch"], TINY["img"], TINY["img"]))
    _MACS[0] = 0
    logits, tokens = vit_forward(img, p, TINY)
    mt = analytic_macs(TINY)
    print(f"instrumented MACs={_MACS[0]:,}  analytic={mt['total']:,}  "
          f"diff={_MACS[0]-mt['total']}")
    assert _MACS[0] == mt["total"]
    print(f"tokens {tokens.shape}, logits[:4] = {logits[0, :4]}")

    # patchify == strided convolution
    if torch is not None:
        P, d, ch = TINY["patch"], TINY["d"], TINY["ch"]
        ref = torch.nn.functional.conv2d(
            torch.tensor(img)[None], torch.tensor(p["pe_w"].reshape(d, ch, P, P)),
            torch.tensor(p["pe_b"]), stride=P)[0].reshape(d, -1).T.numpy()
        ours = patchify(img, p["pe_w"], p["pe_b"], P)
        print(f"patchify vs torch conv2d(stride={P}): max|diff| = "
              f"{np.abs(ours-ref).max():.3e}")
        assert np.abs(ours - ref).max() < 1e-12
    else:
        print("[skipped: torch not installed] strided-conv cross-check")

    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print("PART 2  InfoNCE vs the sigmoid loss")
    print("=" * 74)
    B, D = 8, 6
    Xi = RNG.normal(size=(B, D)); Xt = RNG.normal(size=(B, D))
    tau, bias = 0.07, -10.0
    ls = 1.0 / tau
    f_nce = lambda a, b: infonce(a, b, ls)
    f_sig = lambda a, b: siglip(a, b, ls, bias)
    print(f"batch B={B}, dim={D}, tau={tau} (logit scale {ls:.3f}), sigmoid bias {bias}")
    print(f"  InfoNCE loss = {f_nce(Xi,Xt)[0]:.6f}   sigmoid loss = {f_sig(Xi,Xt)[0]:.6f}")
    e_nce = fd_check(f_nce, Xi, Xt, np.random.default_rng(1))
    e_sig = fd_check(f_sig, Xi, Xt, np.random.default_rng(1))
    print(f"  finite-difference max|error|: InfoNCE {e_nce:.3e}   sigmoid {e_sig:.3e}")
    assert e_nce < 1e-6 and e_sig < 1e-6

    # (a) chunked accumulation over blocks of pairs
    nc = 4
    Zi, Zt = l2n(Xi), l2n(Xt)
    S = Zi @ Zt.T
    A = ls * S + bias
    Zsign = 2.0 * np.eye(B) - 1.0
    part = 0.0
    for a in range(0, B, nc):
        for b in range(0, B, nc):
            sub, zs = A[a:a+nc, b:b+nc], Zsign[a:a+nc, b:b+nc]
            part += -np.log(expit(zs * sub)).sum() / B
    print(f"\n  sigmoid: full {f_sig(Xi,Xt)[0]:.12f}  chunked {part:.12f}  "
          f"|diff| = {abs(part-f_sig(Xi,Xt)[0]):.3e}")
    assert abs(part - f_sig(Xi, Xt)[0]) < 1e-12
    # the same block-local accumulation applied to InfoNCE renormalizes inside
    # each chunk, which is simply the wrong loss
    part_n = 0.0
    for a in range(0, B, nc):
        for b in range(0, B, nc):
            sub = ls * S[a:a+nc, b:b+nc]
            if a == b:
                Pr, Pc = softmax(sub, 1), softmax(sub, 0)
                part_n += -0.5*(np.log(np.diag(Pr)).sum()+np.log(np.diag(Pc)).sum())/B
    print(f"  InfoNCE: full {f_nce(Xi,Xt)[0]:.12f}  chunk-local {part_n:.12f}  "
          f"|diff| = {abs(part_n-f_nce(Xi,Xt)[0]):.3e}")

    # (b) cross-pair coupling: does moving text j change the gradient at text k?
    def cross_coupling(fn, j, k, h=1e-5):
        Xp = Xt.copy(); Xp[j] += h * np.eye(D)[0]
        Xm = Xt.copy(); Xm[j] -= h * np.eye(D)[0]
        gp = fn(Xi, Xp)[2][k]
        gm = fn(Xi, Xm)[2][k]
        return np.abs((gp - gm) / (2 * h)).max()
    c_nce = cross_coupling(f_nce, 3, 5)
    c_sig = cross_coupling(f_sig, 3, 5)
    print(f"\n  d/d(text_3) of grad w.r.t. text_5:  InfoNCE {c_nce:.6e}   "
          f"sigmoid {c_sig:.3e}")
    assert c_nce > 1e-3 and c_sig < 1e-9

    # (c) temperature controls how peaked the negative distribution is
    for t in (1.0, 0.2, 0.07, 0.01):
        Pr = softmax(S / t, axis=1)
        H = float(-(Pr * np.log(Pr + 1e-30)).sum(1).mean())
        print(f"  tau={t:<5} mean row entropy {H:.4f} nats "
              f"(uniform = {np.log(B):.4f}), max off-diag weight "
              f"{(Pr - np.eye(B)*Pr).max():.4f}")
    print("\nall assertions passed.")

It runs in about $1.7$ s. ViT-Base/16 at $224$ prints $197$ tokens, $85{,}798{,}656$ backbone parameters and $17{,}563{,}828{,}224$ MACs, attention matmuls $4.10\%$ of a block; the tiny ViT's built and instrumented counts match their closed forms with difference $0$. Both gradients pass central finite differences at $1.6\times10^{-10}$ and $1.8\times10^{-10}$, and the coupling test gives $7.62\times10^{-2}$ for InfoNCE against exactly $0$ for the sigmoid loss.

Under Encryption

A ViT is a friendlier CKKS target than a decoder language model. The sequence length is fixed at $n=197$ and known before the ciphertext exists, there is no autoregressive loop, and no branch depends on the data — so the whole forward pass is one static circuit, and the $12nd^2$ MACs per block are exactly the matrix multiplications FHE does well. The cost is the non-polynomial residue: $L$ softmaxes (an exponential and a division) and $2L+1$ LayerNorms (an inverse square root). Each needs a polynomial surrogate, each surrogate spends multiplicative depth, and depth accumulates linearly in $L$, so twelve blocks exhaust any realistic budget and force bootstrapping between them. CLIP-style retrieval adds only two $\ell_2$ normalizations per pair, and the $B\times B$ logit matrix is a single matmul — encrypted scoring is cheap; the encoder is the bottleneck. Chapter 39 takes up the approximation problem in detail.

Key Takeaways
  • Patch embedding is a convolution with kernel equal to stride; at $224$ and $P=16$ it yields $196$ patches, $197$ tokens, and ViT-Base's $85.8$M backbone parameters follow from $N = (CP^2{+}1)d + d + nd + L(12d^2{+}13d) + 2d$. Certain
  • ViT's quadratic attention term is negligible at standard resolution — $4.1\%$ of block FLOPs — and only matches the projection term at $n = 6d$, i.e. $4608$ tokens for $d=768$. Certain
  • ViT loses to convnets below roughly ten million images because it must learn locality rather than be given it; augmentation, hard distillation from a convnet teacher, and masked pretraining each recover the gap without touching the architecture. Likely
  • InfoNCE's softmax normalizer couples every pair in the batch, forcing an all-gather and a $B \times B$ logit matrix; the sigmoid loss is a sum of independent per-pair binary problems, so it accumulates chunk-by-chunk with $O(b^2)$ memory and no global reduction. Certain
  • The architecture has been stable since 2020; the frontier is the objective — sigmoid alignment plus captioning and self-distillation in SigLIP 2, Gram anchoring in DINOv3, intermediate-layer alignment in Perception Encoder, and multi-teacher distillation in EUPE. Verify
Chapter 21

State Space Models: S4, Mamba, and the SSD Duality

Learning Objectives
  • Derive the continuous state-space equations $h' = Ah + Bx$, their zero-order-hold discretization, and the convolution kernel $K_\ell = C\bar{A}^\ell\bar{B}$ that the discretization implies.
  • Explain HiPPO initialization as exact online projection onto an orthogonal polynomial basis, and why diagonal-plus-low-rank structure makes the S4 kernel computable in near-linear rather than $O(N^2T)$ time.
  • Explain why making $\Delta$, $B$, $C$ input-dependent destroys time-invariance, forbids the FFT convolution, and forces a hardware-aware parallel scan.
  • State the structured state-space duality — a selective SSM with scalar-identity transitions equals a masked matrix multiply $Y = (L \odot CB^\top)X$ with $L$ 1-semiseparable — and what that equality buys.
  • Implement a selective scan both sequentially and as a Blelloch associative parallel scan in working code, and verify the SSD equality numerically.
Read alongside — the primary papers, still the only complete treatment: Gu, Goel & Ré (S4), Gu & Dao (Mamba), Dao & Gu (Transformers are SSMs, the SSD paper), plus Albert Gu's Goomba Lab blog series, the clearest exposition of the semiseparable-matrix argument anywhere. Prince, Understanding Deep Learning, for the recurrence and convolution background assumed here.

Chapter 17 left recurrence for dead: an RNN's hidden state is a sequential bottleneck, so training cannot be parallelized over time, and the gradient through $T$ nonlinear steps either vanishes or explodes. Chapter 18's transformer traded that for a quadratic-cost attention with no sequential dependence at all. This chapter builds the third option. Take the recurrence, make it linear in the state — no $\tanh$ between steps — and the composition of steps becomes an associative operation, which means the whole sequence can be computed by a parallel scan in $O(\log T)$ depth. That single move recovers RNN inference cost (constant memory per token) with transformer-like training parallelism. Sections 21.1–21.3 build the time-invariant version, where the recurrence collapses to a convolution. Sections 21.4–21.6 simplify the kernel, then make it input-dependent — which is what makes it competitive — and then discover it was a form of attention all along. Section 21.8 says where the line stands.

21.1 Continuous SSMs and Discretization

Start in continuous time with a single-input single-output linear system of order $N$:

$$h'(t) = A\,h(t) + B\,x(t), \qquad y(t) = C\,h(t) + D\,x(t),$$

with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$, $C \in \mathbb{R}^{1\times N}$. This is the control theorist's object, standard since Kalman's state-space formulation around 1960. Its exact solution is the variation-of-constants formula $h(t) = e^{A(t-t_0)}h(t_0) + \int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-\tau)}B\,x(\tau)\,d\tau$. Deep learning consumes discrete tokens, so we need a discrete recurrence, and the discretization is where the learnable timescale enters.

Definition 21.1 (Zero-order hold discretization)

Fix a step $\Delta > 0$ and assume the input is piecewise constant, $x(\tau) = x_k$ for $\tau \in [k\Delta, (k+1)\Delta)$. Substituting into variation of constants over one step gives $h_{k+1} = \bar{A}h_k + \bar{B}x_k$ exactly, with $$\bar{A} = e^{\Delta A}, \qquad \bar{B} = \Big(\int_0^{\Delta} e^{As}\,ds\Big)B = A^{-1}\big(e^{\Delta A} - I\big)B .$$ The output map is unchanged: $y_k = Ch_k + Dx_k$. ZOH is exact for piecewise-constant inputs, unlike the bilinear or Euler alternatives, and it preserves stability: $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda(A) < 0 \iff |\lambda(\bar A)| < 1$.

Now unroll from $h_{-1}=0$. Because the recurrence is linear and $\bar A, \bar B, C$ do not depend on $k$, the map from input sequence to output sequence is a convolution:

$$h_k = \sum_{j=0}^{k} \bar{A}^{\,k-j}\bar{B}x_j \;\Longrightarrow\; y_k = \sum_{j=0}^{k} \underbrace{\big(C\bar{A}^{\,k-j}\bar{B}\big)}_{K_{k-j}} x_j + Dx_k, \qquad K_\ell = C\bar{A}^{\,\ell}\bar{B}.$$

$K \in \mathbb{R}^{T}$ is the SSM convolution kernel: a causal FIR filter as long as the sequence, generated by only $O(N)$ parameters. Training runs the convolution, which FFT computes in $O(T\log T)$; inference runs the recurrence, which costs $O(N)$ state and $O(N)$ work per token with no cache that grows in $T$. Two algorithms, one model.

Example 21.1 (A first-order kernel by hand)

Take $N=1$, $A=-1$, $B=C=1$, $\Delta = 0.5$. Then $\bar A = e^{-0.5} = 0.606531$ and $\bar B = (-1)^{-1}(e^{-0.5}-1) = 0.393469$. The kernel is $K_0 = 0.393469$, $K_1 = 0.606531 \times 0.393469 = 0.238651$, $K_2 = 0.367879 \times 0.393469 = 0.144749$, a decaying exponential. Its total mass is $\sum_\ell K_\ell = \bar B/(1-\bar A) = 0.393469/0.393469 = 1$, which must equal the continuous DC gain $-CA^{-1}B = 1$. Halving $\Delta$ to $0.25$ gives $\bar A = 0.778801$: the same continuous system, a slower-decaying discrete kernel, twice the effective memory in steps. $\Delta$ is the timescale knob. Certain

21.2 HiPPO and Principled Initialization

A randomly initialized $A$ produces a kernel that either decays within a handful of steps or blows up; in S4 this was the entire difference between a layer that solves Path-X and one that is at chance. The right initialization answers a different question: what is the optimal $N$-dimensional online summary of everything seen so far?

Theorem 21.1 (HiPPO-LegS, Gu et al. 2020)

Let $x: \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\to\mathbb{R}$ and let $c(t) \in \mathbb{R}^N$ be the coefficients of the orthogonal projection of $x|_{[0,t]}$ onto the span of the first $N$ Legendre polynomials rescaled to $[0,t]$, under the uniform measure on that interval. Then $c(t)$ satisfies exactly the linear ODE $$\frac{d}{dt}c(t) = -\frac{1}{t}A\,c(t) + \frac{1}{t}B\,x(t), \qquad A_{nk} = \begin{cases}(2n+1)^{1/2}(2k+1)^{1/2} & n > k\\ n+1 & n = k \\ 0 & n < k\end{cases}, \quad B_n = (2n+1)^{1/2}.$$

Proof sketch. Differentiate the projection coefficient $c_n(t) = \int_0^t x(s)\,p_n^{(t)}(s)\,ds$ under the integral sign. The basis itself moves with $t$, so the derivative picks up a term $\int_0^t x(s)\,\partial_t p_n^{(t)}(s)\,ds$; the Legendre three-term recurrence lets $\partial_t p_n^{(t)}$ be re-expanded in $\{p_k^{(t)}\}_{k\le n}$, and collecting coefficients gives exactly the lower-triangular $A$ above. The ODE is exact, not a first-order approximation: no error term is dropped. (What is approximate is the $N$-term projection itself; its dynamics are not.) $\blacksquare$

The consequence is that a state-space layer initialized at the HiPPO matrix begins life as a provably optimal compressor of its own history, and gradient descent then deforms it toward whatever the task actually needs — Chapter 17's unanswered question of what a recurrent memory should be at step zero. Likely that the specific measure matters less than having some principled long-memory structure; later work (Section 21.4) found much simpler initializations work nearly as well.

HiPPO-LegS is lower-triangular and badly non-normal. Diagonalizing it is numerically catastrophic: S4 derives the explicit diagonalization and finds that the eigenvector matrix $V$ has binomial entries growing to magnitude $2^{4N/3}$ — about $5\times10^{25}$ at $N=64$, far past what fp64's sixteen digits absorb. But it decomposes as normal-plus-low-rank, $A = A^{(\mathrm{N})} - PQ^\top$ with $\mathrm{rank}(PQ^\top)=1$, and the normal part is unitarily diagonalizable. Conjugating gives the diagonal-plus-low-rank (DPLR) form $A = V\Lambda V^{*} - PQ^{*}$.

21.3 S4: the Convolution View

Computing $K_\ell = C\bar A^\ell \bar B$ for $\ell = 0,\dots,T-1$ naively costs $O(N^2T)$ time and $O(NT)$ memory — a nonstarter at $N=64$, $T=16{,}384$. S4's contribution is an algorithm that exploits DPLR structure to get it in $\tilde{O}(N+T)$.

The route is the frequency domain. Define the truncated generating function $\hat K(z) = \sum_{\ell=0}^{T-1}K_\ell z^\ell$. Evaluating $\hat K$ at the $T$ roots of unity and applying an inverse FFT recovers $K$, so it suffices to evaluate $\hat K$ at $T$ points. Summing the geometric series gives $\hat K(z) = \tilde C(I - z\bar A)^{-1}\bar B$ where $\tilde C$ absorbs the truncation correction $(I - \bar A^T)$. The resolvent $(I - z\bar A)^{-1}$ of a DPLR matrix is handled by the Woodbury identity: for rank-one $P,Q$,

$$(\Lambda - PQ^{*})^{-1} = \Lambda^{-1} + \Lambda^{-1}P\big(1 - Q^{*}\Lambda^{-1}P\big)^{-1}Q^{*}\Lambda^{-1},$$

which reduces every evaluation to four sums of the form $\sum_{n} \frac{u_n v_n}{\omega - \lambda_n}$. That is a Cauchy kernel, computable for all $T$ frequencies at once in $O((N+T)\log^2(N+T))$ by fast multipole methods, or $O(NT)$ by brute force with tiny constants. The bill: $\tilde O(N+T)$ to build the kernel, $O(T\log T)$ to apply it.

21.4 Diagonal SSMs and Gating

Then DSS and S4D showed the low-rank correction is nearly dispensable. Drop $PQ^*$, keep a complex diagonal $A = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N)$ in conjugate pairs so the kernel stays real, and initialize the poles on a line: S4D-Lin sets $\lambda_n = -\tfrac12 + i\pi n$. The kernel becomes a single matrix of powers, $K_\ell = 2\,\mathrm{Re}\sum_n C_n\bar B_n\bar\lambda_n^{\,\ell}$, computable directly — no Woodbury, no Cauchy kernel, twenty lines of code. Long Range Arena accuracy barely moves.

Since $\bar\lambda_n^\ell = e^{-\alpha_n \ell}e^{i\omega_n\ell}$, the kernel is a sum of $N$ damped sinusoids. An S4D layer is a learned bank of damped-oscillator filters, parameterized by decay rate and frequency rather than by $T$ free taps. That is why it has long memory with few parameters, and also why it is weak at anything content-addressed: the filter bank is fixed once trained, so what it attends to is a function of offset, never of content.

H3 fixed a specific failure — associative recall, the induction-head task of Chapter 18 — by pairing a shift-SSM with a diagonal SSM and a multiplicative gate. The Mamba block simplified this to: expand the residual stream by a factor of 2, apply a short causal depthwise conv1d and SiLU, run the SSM, gate elementwise against a second SiLU branch, project back. The conv1d matters more than it looks; it supplies the short-range mixing the SSM is bad at.

21.5 Mamba: Selective State Spaces

LTI is a hard ceiling. A convolution's response to a token depends only on that token's distance from the output position, so the layer cannot decide that this token is a name worth remembering and that one is a comma worth forgetting: nothing reads content before the state update is chosen. Attention's entire content is that mechanism.

Definition 21.2 (Selective SSM)
